title: Lesson 12: Change Management as a Deliverable, Not an Afterthought
description: Treating each meaningful change to a live delivery as its own bounded deliverable with a scope, a named risk, a test, a rollback, and a record, instead of a drive-by edit that quietly erodes a working system.

questions.question: Per the lesson about change management as a deliverable, what is the central focus?
options: Treating change to a live delivery as its own deliverable with scope, risk, test, rollback, and record, not a drive-by edit
A review of unrelated config tools
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a live delivery drifts one small unrecorded edit at a time unless change is treated as a bounded, visible deliverable.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: A drive-by edit feels small because nothing breaks visibly, so it needs no record
Bundling extra unrequested edits into an approved change is efficient and harmless
Scope the change like a mini-engagement: what changes, what does not, who approves, and how to roll back
Trust your own judgment over a test because you built the original
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that each meaningful change answers the same questions as the original build in miniature, turning a drive-by edit into a visible deliverable.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The rollback plan is improvised after the change lands
The rollback is the most important artifact and must be written before the change, specific to the exact prior state
A change to a system that runs itself needs no gates because nobody is watching anyway
Tell the client about a high-risk change after it lands since the output looks the same
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a change that cannot be rolled back cleanly is a change you cannot afford to be wrong about, so the revert is written before the change.
